hooks.text: When scientists first saw a platypus, they thought it was fake.
The first scientists to examine a platypus attacked it with scissors.
In 1799, naturalists received a preserved animal they insisted was stitched together.

title: When Scientists Thought the Platypus Was a Fake
description: In 1799, the first scientists to examine a platypus thought it was a fake hoax sewn together.

beats.text: When scientists first saw a platypus, they thought it was completely fake.
beats.visual: Museum specimen of a platypus in Natural History Museum London

beats.text: In 1799, naturalist George Shaw produced the first formal description in the Naturalists Miscellany.
beats.visual: George Shaw Naturalist's Miscellany plate of the duck-billed platypus

beats.text: Convinced the specimen was stitched together by Asian artisans, he took a sharp pair of scissors to the pelt.
beats.visual: Historical scientific illustration of platypus pelt from 19th century

beats.text: Finding no hidden stitches, he reluctantly named it Platypus anatinus.
beats.visual: Ornithorhynchus anatinus swimming in an Australian freshwater stream

beats.text: Decades later, William Hay Caldwell confirmed that this remarkable mammal actually lays leathery eggs.
beats.visual: Historical scientific illustration of platypus eggs

beats.text: Even stranger, they hunt underwater completely blind, using electrolocation to detect every single prey.
beats.visual: Ornithorhynchus anatinus bill detail showing electroreceptors

beats.text: And under ultraviolet light, their thick fur remarkably glows a vibrant cyan and green.
beats.visual: Platypus under ultraviolet light showing biofluorescence
